body.text: Inquest into baby deaths hears homebirths have doubled since COVID
In the midst of two weeks of heartbreaking testimony about what can go wrong when babies are born outside hospitals, a stark piece of evidence emerged.
A coronial inquest heard the number of babies delivered by homebirth has doubled in Australia since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Deputy Coroner Joan Baptie is investigating the deaths of three babies born by freebirth in northern New South Wales, and a fourth by homebirth in the Hunter Valley.
A homebirth is when a woman plans to have her baby at home under the care of a registered midwife who works in the private sector or is employed by a hospital.
In NSW, up to 600 babies are now born at a midwife-assisted homebirth each year, up from about 280 in 2019.

A freebirth, sometimes referred to as an unassisted birth, is different from a homebirth in that there is no-one with medical training in the room and the mother often has had no medical support through her pregnancy, though some do opt for antenatal care with a medical professional.
There is currently no data on the number of freebirths.
A 'marked distrust'
The court heard non-clinical and often controversial approaches to birthing were widely shared on the internet and social media.
Doctor Andrew Bisits, from the Royal Hospital for Women, told the court that material was a "contemporary factor" that influenced birthing decisions.
"These could really drive someone's decision … [and are] very supportive of those controversial decisions," he said.
"There is a marked distrust and hostility toward anything viewed as establishment that will ride over their autonomy."
Dr Bisits said medical practitioners needed to adapt to the changing world and find ways to address women's concerns.
"Resentment [about alternative views] is useless,"
Dr Bisits said women had the right to choose how they gave birth, but it was the clinician's role to ensure they made an informed decision.
'Things we need to fix'
Western Sydney University midwifery professor Hannah Dahlen told the court mistrust of the hospital system, past trauma and cost were some of the reasons for birthing at home.
"We have a lot of things we need to fix within our system," she said.
"We have very high intervention rates; we have more and more women seeking a physiological and relationship-based care model."
Little lives lost
For the past two weeks, the coroner has heard evidence about the deaths of three babies born by freebirth in northern NSW, and a fourth by homebirth in the Hunter Valley.
The court heard about the advice given to the mothers before, during and after the births.
The inquest heard two "birth keepers" who attended the three freebirths did not have medical qualifications.
Birth keeper Sita Kali was at the births of Baby R in 2022 and Baby D in 2024. The babies and their families cannot be named for legal reasons.

The court heard Ms Kali had recalculated the birthdate of Baby R's mother from the date of conception, rather than the medically accepted practice of using the date of the mother's last menstrual period.
This meant Ms Kali had advised the mother her baby was due two weeks later than indicated during an earlier clinical visit.
At 43-weeks gestation, Baby R's mother had an ultrasound and was advised by the sonographer that she needed immediate medical care and was told to go to the Tweed Hospital immediately.
The court heard the mother turned to Ms Kali for advice despite knowing she had no medical training.
Counsel assisting the coroner, Ragni Mathur, said the birth keeper noted the woman's anxiety and advised her to go home to calm down before making a decision.
Within hours, the woman had gone into labour. The baby was born with the cord around its neck, had breathing difficulties and faeces on its face.
Twelve hours later, emergency services were called, but the baby died.
In a statement after the baby died, the mother said: "I was afraid to go to hospital and be forced into a caesarean. I still thought the baby was OK".
Baby R died from complications arising from "severe post-maturity".
Baby D
Baby D died in 2024, hours after his birth and following the delivery of his stillborn twin.
Their mother had no prenatal medical care and did not know she was having twins.
The cause of death was believed to be twin-to-twin transfusion, a complication arising from sharing a placenta.

Ms Kali told the court the knowledge she drew on when assisting the women came from her lived experience, and reading and sharing stories with Indigenous elders, shamans, grandmothers and other birth keepers.
"Midwifery is as old as humans. Clinical midwifery is modern medicine,"
she said.
Baby DH
The court heard a post-mortem revealed Baby DH died in 2024 from severe and complex congenital cardiac abnormalities.
Expert reports tendered to court said while the baby could not have survived without specialised care, the death "was not inevitable".
Baby DH's mother did not access clinical antenatal care throughout the pregnancy, instead choosing a freebirth and engaging the services of birth keeper Amy Lou Smith.
In her evidence, Ms Smith said she would have supported the mother seeking medical assistance if she asked for it.
But the parents did not agree with that evidence.
The court heard that in an interview with police, the parents said they raised concerns with Ms Smith numerous times about the purple colour of the baby, his "floppiness" and his breathing.
Safer births
Medical experts told the inquest that the babies born by freebirth would likely have survived if their conditions were detected in early pregnancy.
Professor Dahlen told the court that with medical intervention, the twins would "both probably have survived, but not without risk".
Her evidence, and that of fellow midwife Alison Teate, was that antenatal care would have detected two babies sharing a placenta, making it a "very high-risk" birth.

Professor Dahlen said respecting a mother's right to choose, offering continuity of care and creating a community liaison midwife could help bridge the widening gap between non-clinical and clinical birth practices.
"It's a clever way to reach across the divide to connect the two sides that are not communicating," she said.
"We have to engage birth keepers and doulas; we have to work together.
"It's surely about the safety and positive experiences of that woman and her baby."
The deputy coroner will now consider the evidence and deliver her findings and recommendations at a later date.
